messages.subject: SAM approach with categorical indicators
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone.

I'm a phd student.

After reading again the Rossel and Loh paper (2022) about sam approach I realized it was developed assuming continuous and latent variable indicators. So, I was thinking if this approach would make sense in case my items are categorical:

1) To run a sem model with binary items with their corresponding thresholds, which indeed are assumed to be continuous.
2) Then, estimate the parameters with the sam approach.

The issue I found is about the interpretation of the coefficients. Any suggestions?

messages.subject_clean: semTools::measEq.syntax - Error: no method for coercing this S4 class to a vector
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am working on measurement invariance analysis using semTools to create syntax for multi-group CFA with categorical indicators (MI across biological sex, 2 groups).

I have been using the very useful measEq.syntax-function until now. However. since beginning of March I cannot execute my syntax anymore.  I have tried a lot of troubleshooting options (see below) - none worked.

Here is example code and exemplary error presentation:
 fit <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mod.cat <http://mod.cat>, data = df_mi_parent,
                            ordered = c("item1", "item2", "item3", ...., "item25"),
                            group = "sex",group.label=c("1", "2"),
                            estimator ="DWLS",
                            test = "scaled.shifted",
                            se = "robust",
                            parameterization = "theta",
                            ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                            group.equal = "thresholds")
# Runs perfectly

summary(syntax.thresh)                    # summarize model features
Length Class Mode 1 measEq.syntax S4
mod.thresh <- as.character(syntax.thresh) # save as text
Error in as.character.default(syntax.thresh) : no method for coercing this S4 class to a vector
cat(mod.thresh)  # print/view lavaan syntax
# cannot be executed since line above was aborted.

I have attempted the following troubleshooting approaches. Unfirtunately, all have been  unsuccessful.

1. updated R, lavaan and semTools
2. Followed this: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/63065696/error-in-getmethodsummary-signature-fitdiff/63600180#63600180
3. also tried this, loading semTools (not loading lavaan first etc.): https://github.com/simsem/semTools/issues/116
4. Rerun all following this example: https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/semTools/versions/0.5-6/topics/measEq.syntax

I would highly appreciate some help on how to overcome the S4 issue. I am not an R-programmer and therefore have a limited understanding of the S3/S4 classesd/objects. I am an applied researcher - Hence, I appreciate any help I solve the issue using semTools or any workaround.

Thanks in advance, I am happy to provide more information or code and hope this follows the community guidelines.

Best

Claudia

messages.subject: Re: RI-CLPM within-centered variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nina,

In the RI-CLPM, a latent factor is created for each observed variable across time. The multiplication of 1 by the variable is for identification purposes when constructing the latent factor. There are also some constraints you have to place on residuals, which is also reflected in the code from that website. From an analysis standpoint, you are interested in the relationships among the latent factors; that is where you specify your autoregressive and cross-lagged paths.

Hope that helps.

Best,

Ryan

messages.subject: Smaller degrees of freedom for the Scalar invariance model than that of the Metric one?
messages.subject_clean: Smaller degrees of freedom for the Scalar invariance model than that of the Metric one?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am trying to test the measurement invariance in my bi-factor model with CFA tests. I have 23 binary questions coded "correct" and "incorrect" and 3 different groups in my data. The sample sizes are approximately 200 for each group.
To test the measurement invariance, I have followed the Van de Schoot et al. (2012) step-by-step process where progressively constrained models are compared. I have estimated the configural, metric and scalar model. The test statistics, fit indices and model results all seem good and reasonable. However, when I estimate the Scalar model, results give smaller degrees of freedom than the metric model.
Is there a possible reason for this? I couldn't find anything in the internet although I looked for it carefully. Can someone please assist me to find the reason or help me to find a reference to have a better understanding?

Here are the codes that I run.
### configural model ###
model_mck_bifactor_con_2 <- 'MCK =~ Q1+Q2A+Q3B+Q3C+Q5+Q6+Q8A+Q8B+Q8C+Q10+Q12B+Q13A+Q13B+Q13C+Q17A+Q18B+Q19A+Q19B+Q19C+Q19D+Q20A+Q22+Q23
Q8 =~ Q8A+Q8B+Q8C; Q13 =~ Q13A+Q13B+Q13C; Q19 =~ Q19A+Q19B+Q19C+Q19D;
MCK~~0*Q8; MCK~~0*Q13; MCK~~0*Q19;
Q8~~0*Q13; Q8~~0*Q19; Q13~~0*Q19
Q3B ~~ Q19A+Q19B+Q19C+Q19D; Q3C ~~ Q19A+Q19B+Q19C+Q19D; Q3B ~~ Q3C'
### Q3 and Q19 are theoretically correlated. ###

cfa.configural.mck.bifactor_2 <- cfa(model_mck_bifactor_con_2, data = data_mck, estimator = "WLSMV", ordered=T, group = "COUNTRY",
                                     missing="pairwise", parameterization="delta")

### metric model ###
cfa.metric.mck.bifactor <- cfa(model_mck_bifactor_con_2, data = data_mck, estimator = "WLSMV", ordered=T, group = "COUNTRY", missing="pairwise",
  parameterization="delta", group.equal="loadings")
summary(cfa.metric.mck.bifactor, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

### scalar model ###
cfa.scalar.mck.bifactor <- cfa(model_mck_bifactor_con_2, data = data_mck, estimator = "WLSMV", ordered=T, group = "COUNTRY", missing="pairwise",
                               parameterization="delta", group.equal=c("loadings","thresholds"))

Below is the compareFit test results. As you can see, the scalar model has smaller Df.

Thanks a lot in advance.
I wish everyone a good and productive day.
Best Regards,
Enes.

messages.subject: SEM with 50% missing data (due to distribution of items over various ballots/waves)
messages.subject_clean: SEM with 50% missing data (due to distribution of items over various ballots/waves)
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I want to test a multilevel mediation (particularly, test a number of hypotheses about possible mediators of the effect of social class on Right-Wing Authoritarianism) using largely categorical variables surveyed in the General Social Survey, and for this, I would have liked to use Structural Equation Modeling. However, I have doubts about its feasibility, due to missing data.

In fact, there is not a single participant with data on all variables I want to include, because the items were each asked in different waves or ballots. For example, I would have one item that was only asked in ballots A and B, a second item that only occured in ballots B and C, and a third in ballots A and C. Because I am dealing with categorical data, I am considering WLSMV in Mplus, which uses pairwise deletion. In theory, I can draw up a covariance matrix, since every variable co-occurs with every other variable in one ballot or another: for each pair of variables (so for each covariance I need), I have at least 900 participants (though out of a total of more than 10.000 participants). Therefore, intuitively, using list-wise deletion does not seem very problematic to me, since most missings should be MCAR (they result from randomization in the administration of certain ballots/modules) - with perhaps the exception of a few variables that were not asked in particular years/waves. However, when I read about this, it is often recommended that list-wise deletion is not justified when you have more than 10% missings (a threshold that I far exceed here).

Is there a method of dealing with missings that allows me to estimate this model, even though each respondent has randomly missing data on around 50% of the variables? Or is it not feasible/advisable to use SEM in my case?

Thank you in advance for any guidance!

messages.subject: model specification second-order
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,
this is my first time trying to specify a CFA. My research question is, whether there is a shared underlying mechanism (=sensitization) behind 10 different measures. So I have 10 measures (= manifest variables), divided in two cognitive-behavioral, three psychophysiological and five neural measures. This is what I specified so far in lavaan:

CFAmodel <- 'cognitivebehavioral =~ AAT_bias_smoking + IAT_app_av_score
             EMG =~ EMGcorr_score + EMGzygo_score + EMGstartle_score
             fMRI =~ ACC + lAG + rThal + rStriatum + lSTG
             sensitization =~ cognitivebehavioral + EMG + fMRI'

Unfortunately, I receive the following error message:

> CFAmodel_a <- cfa(CFAmodel, data_CFA, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)  Warnmeldung: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats, : lavaan WARNING: Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not identified.

Can somebody help? If I am not wrong, the model should be identified. I was thinking about fixing all paths of the first-order latent variables to 1, because I am only interested in the second-order variable.

Best,
Franziska

messages.subject: Re: model specification second-order
messages.body_plain:
Dear Franziska,

if I were you, I would try to reduce the model to localize the error.
First, are the variable names written correctly?
Second, try to eliminate the std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE statement because it seems you use the marker indicator approach to identifiy the factors (aka give factors the metric of the first variable each). If you use the "fix factor variance to 1" approach, try to eliminate the  1* - statement and leave std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE in the specification.
Third, if you have checked the above hints, try to fit a cfa only with two of the factors, if the problem persists, try a combination of two other factors and so on.
I don't know your data, but consider using estimator = "MLR" (https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/est.html) since the data is probably skewed (check with describe(data_CFA)

Hope that helps.

Kindly,
Marcus

Dear Marcus,
thank you, that has already taken me a step further! Now, my model specification looks like this:

### Prepare Data (e.g., standardize and flip to the expected direction)
data_CFA <- subset(data, select=c(AAT_bias_smoking, IAT_app_av_score, IAT_val_score, EMGcorr_score, EMGzygo_score, EMGstartle_score, ACC, lAG, rThal, rStriatum, lSTG))
data_CFA <- as.data.frame(apply(data_CFA,  2, scale)) # apply scale to all columns to centralize and standardize: mean = 0 & SD = 1
# higher scores mean higher sensitization in all measures
data_CFA$EMGcorr_score <- data_CFA$EMGcorr_score * (-1)
data_CFA$EMGstartle_score <- data_CFA$EMGstartle_score * (-1)
data_CFA$lSTG <- data_CFA$lSTG * (-1)

CFAmodel <- '# measurement model
             cognitivebehavioral =~ AAT_bias_smoking + IAT_app_av_score + IAT_val_score

             EMG =~ EMGcorr_score + EMGzygo_score + EMGstartle_score
             fMRI =~ ACC + lAG + rThal + rStriatum + lSTG
             sensitization =~ cognitivebehavioral + EMG + fMRI

             # structural model
             ACC ~~ lAG
             ACC ~~ rThal
             ACC ~~ rStriatum
             ACC ~~ lSTG
             lAG ~~ rThal
             lAG ~~ rStriatum
             lAG ~~ lSTG
             rThal ~~ rStriatum
             rThal ~~ lSTG
             rStriatum ~~ lSTG
             IAT_app_av_score ~~ IAT_val_score
             EMGcorr_score ~~ EMGzygo_score
             EMGcorr_score ~~ EMGstartle_score
             EMGstartle_score ~~ EMGzygo_score
            '
CFAmodel_a <- cfa(CFAmodel, data_CFA, estimator = "MLR", missing = "FIML", std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE) # adressing missing values and skewed data

summary(CFAmodel_a, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized=TRUE)

I added covariances between measures which were collected within the same task, since they should share a certain amount of variance.

However, again, I run into many warning messages... (also without the added covariances)
Warning messages: 1: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats, : lavaan WARNING: The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov) does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue (= -6.731629e-04) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that the model is not identified. 2: In lav_object_post_check(object) : lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative

The problem is, that simplifying the model (e.g., consider only two factors) would mean that I can not answer my research questions, whether all measures share an underlying mechanism (i.e., sensitization).

Does anyone has a tip how to deals with this issues?

Best,
Franziska

messages.subject: Re: model specification second-order
messages.body_plain:
You don't need the covariances between measures (in general); they are supposed to be explained by the latent factors (unless some specific observable variables need to be related to one another, beyond what the latent factors explain). The problem with the model underidentification may be due to that.

Refer to my previous message (yesterday) to see how you can deal with your original underidentification.

Best,
--
Daniel Morillo, Ph.D.
GitHub <https://github.com/DaniMori> |  ORCID <https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3021-3878>

messages.subject: How to visualize a complex Bifactor SEM with Third-order Factor?
messages.subject_clean: How to visualize a complex Bifactor SEM with Third-order Factor?
messages.body_plain:
Hello, good day to everyone

I'm working on visualizing a complex bifactor Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) in R with a third-order factor (AUTOREGULACION) and several nested factors. I've run into issues with layout when trying to represent the model graphically using semPlot. The model includes first-order factors (F1 to F11), second-order factors (PLANIFICACION, EJECUCION, AUTOEVALUACION), and a third-order factor that encompasses the second-order factors. Here's the lavaan package syntax for my model:

´´´
model_AF <- '
 # First Order Factors
 F1 =~ P3 + P4 + P9 + P10 + P13 + P14 + P15 + P20
 F2 =~ P6 + P8 + P11 + P12 + P16 + P17 + P18 + P19 + P22 + P26
 F3 =~ P1 + P2 + P5 + P7
 F4 =~ P21 + P23 + P24 + P25
 F5 =~ P27 + P28 + P29 + P30 + P31 + P33 + P40
 F6 =~ P34 + P37 + P39 + P41 + P43
 F7 =~ P36 + P38 + P42 + P44
 F8 =~ P32 + P35
 F9 =~ P50 + P51 + P52 + P53 + P54 + P55 + P56 + P57 + P58 + P58 + P59
 F10 =~ P45 + P46 + P47 + P48 + P49 + P61
 F11 =~ P60 + P62

 # Second Order Factors
 PLANIFICACION =~ 1*F1 + 1*F2 + 1*F3 + 1*F4
 EJECUCION =~ 1*F5 + 1*F6 + 1*F7 + 1*F8
 AUTOEVALUACION =~ 1*F9 + 1*F10 + 1*F11

 # Third Order Factor
 AUTOREGULACION =~ 1*PLANIFICACION + 1*EJECUCION + 1*AUTOEVALUACION AUTOREGULACION ~~ AUTOREGULACION '

 model_fit <- cfa(model_AF, data = base, orthogonal = FALSE) semPaths(model_fit, whatLabels="est", layout="tree", rotation=2)
´´´

2nd order

3th order

What are the best practices for visualizing such a complex SEM? Are there specific semPlot parameters or other R packages that could handle this level of complexity better?

I hope you can help me

messages.subject: Re: model specification second-order
messages.body_plain:
It seems like my first message didn't get through (or it doesn't appear in the message list in the Google group at least). My last one may seem cryptic if so... This is what I was saying:

The only part that is (locally) underidentified is the "cognitivebehavioral" latent variable, as it is measured by only two indicators. So you need to add a restriction as you correctly did to one of the parameters, i.e. fixing the loading of AAT_bias_smoking to 1. The rest of the fixed parameters may be adding to many restrictions that the fitted model cannot properly accommodate.

You can try freeing those parameters and leaving only the restriction needed for identification, i.e.:

CFAmodel <- 'cognitivebehavioral =~ 1*AAT_bias_smoking + IAT_app_av_score

             EMG =~ EMGcorr_score + EMGzygo_score + EMGstartle_score
             fMRI =~ ACC + lAG + rThal + rStriatum + lSTG

             sensitization =~ cognitivebehavioral + EMG + fMRI'

Hope that helps!

--
Daniel Morillo, Ph.D.
GitHub <https://github.com/DaniMori> |  ORCID <https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3021-3878>

messages.subject: Re: SEM with 50% missing data (due to distribution of items over various ballots/waves)
messages.subject_clean: SEM with 50% missing data (due to distribution of items over various ballots/waves)
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

SEM-approach is very well suited for your purpose.
It seems to me that you used a planned missing design. So, multiple imputation would be your friend dealing with this kind of missingness, see Gonzalez & Rutkowski, 2010. In own studies, we use a balanced incomplete matrix booklet design and applied Multiple Imputation via MICE (see https://osf.io/wa6bn; there is a link to the postprint ).
You can try using fitting a model first with pairwise missing (maybe using the PWL-estimator? as outlined here: https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html) and compare those results with the results of the model with Multiple Imputations, maybe as a kind of sensitivity analysis. But, your sample size is quiet large, so you will have a lot of options experimenting with that.

Hope, that helps.

kindly,
Marcus

th.va...@gmail.com schrieb am Freitag, 5. April 2024 um 21:34:44 UTC+2:
> Dear all,
>
> I want to test a multilevel mediation (particularly, test a number of hypotheses about possible mediators of the effect of social class on Right-Wing Authoritarianism) using largely categorical variables surveyed in the General Social Survey, and for this, I would have liked to use Structural Equation Modeling. However, I have doubts about its feasibility, due to missing data.
>
> In fact, there is not a single participant with data on all variables I want to include, because the items were each asked in different waves or ballots. For example, I would have one item that was only asked in ballots A and B, a second item that only occured in ballots B and C, and a third in ballots A and C. Because I am dealing with categorical data, I am considering WLSMV in Mplus, which uses pairwise deletion. In theory, I can draw up a covariance matrix, since every variable co-occurs with every other variable in one ballot or another: for each pair of variables (so for each covariance I need), I have at least 900 participants (though out of a total of more than 10.000 participants). Therefore, intuitively, using list-wise deletion does not seem very problematic to me, since most missings should be MCAR (they result from randomization in the administration of certain ballots/modules) - with perhaps the exception of a few variables that were not asked in particular years/waves. However, when I read about this, it is often recommended that list-wise deletion is not justified when you have more than 10% missings (a threshold that I far exceed here).
>
> Is there a method of dealing with missings that allows me to estimate this model, even though each respondent has randomly missing data on around 50% of the variables? Or is it not feasible/advisable to use SEM in my case?
>
> Thank you in advance for any guidance!

messages.body_plain:
Thanks again to both of you for your help! This makes perfect sense. I separated the model for simplicity and ran 3 cfa's, one each for cognitive-behavioral, EMG, and fMRI measures:

### COGNITIVE-BEHAVIORAL
CFAmodel_CB <- 'cognitivebehavioral =~  IAT_app_av_score + AAT_bias_smoking + IAT_val_score'
summary(CFAmodel_CB_output, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
Warning message: In lav_object_post_check(object) : lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative
### EMG
CFAmodel_EMG <- 'EMG =~ EMGstartle_score + EMGzygo_score + EMGcorr_score'
CFAmodel_EMG_output <- cfa(CFAmodel_EMG, data_CFA, missing = "FIML")
summary(CFAmodel_EMG_output, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
Warning message: In lav_object_post_check(object) : lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative
### fMRI
CFAmodel_fMRI <- 'fMRI =~ ACC + lAG + rThal + rStriatum + lSTG'
CFAmodel_fMRI_output <- cfa(CFAmodel_fMRI, data_CFA, missing = "FIML")#, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE
summary(CFAmodel_fMRI_output, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
--> works!

The error messages for the models of the cognitive-behavioral and EMG measures also occur when using only complete cases (cognitive-behavioral: n = 348, EMG: n = 173). I read some common reasons for this problem (e.g. underidentification, missing data, manifest variables have different scales, skewed data), but I think I addressed all these possibilities (I standardized the data, used only complete cases, tried all robust estimators on complete case analysis, and the model should not be underidentified). So if you have an idea, let me know.

However, I think I have found a reasonable solution, unless I have misunderstood something. I have specified this model:
CFAmodel_full <- 'cognitivebehavioral =~ 1/3*AAT_bias_smoking + 1/3*IAT_app_av_score + 1/3*IAT_val_score
             EMG =~ 1/3*EMGcorr_score + 1/3*EMGzygo_score + 1/3*EMGstartle_score
             fMRI =~ 1/5*ACC + 1/5*rThal + 1/5*rStriatum + 1/5*lSTG + 1/5*lAG

             sensitization =~ cognitivebehavioral + EMG + fMRI'

CFAmodel_full_output <- cfa(CFAmodel_full, data_CFA, missing = "FIML", std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)
summary(CFAmodel_full_output, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized=TRUE)

This works without an error message, and I think it answers my research question of whether there is a common mechanism among all 11 measures separated at the cognitive-behavioral, psychophysical (EMG), and neural (fMRI) level. I assign equal loadings to the manifest variables because I am not interested in those loadings anyway. I am only interested in the estimates between the first and second order latent variables. I also think the results make sense. All of the fMRI measures are moderately correlated (as I know from simple correlational analyses), whereas the EMG and cognitive-behavioral measures are not. Thus, the fMRI measures share a large amount of variance, and therefore the second order variable "contains" this variance, leading to the highest estimate.
Latent Variables: Estimate Std.Err z-value P(>|z|) Std.lv Std.all sensitization =~
cognitivebhvrl -0.208 0.166 -1.248 0.212 -0.203 -0.203 EMG -0.157 0.201 -0.781 0.435 -0.155 -0.155 fMRI 3.469 0.308 11.259 0.000 0.961 0.961

If you have any concerns about this solution, please let me know.
Best,
Franziska

messages.subject: Re: SEM with 50% missing data (due to distribution of items over various ballots/waves)
messages.subject_clean: SEM with 50% missing data (due to distribution of items over various ballots/waves)
messages.body_plain:
Dear Thomas,

I am not an expert on MI, but what I have read is quite promising. 50% of missingness, especially if it is a planned missing data design (and in your case, you have a very high N), I do not see any problems. Just consider to use an appropriate numer of imputations and iterations. It is more important to analyze (or better, to know) if the data is MCAR, MAR or MNAR and to analyze the missingness patterns - are these pattens random or do they depend upon certain variables?

Maybe you find some additional information here:

https://www.peterlugtig.com/post/planned-missingness/

I would refer you to this manuals and ressources:
- https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/149140/how-much-missing-data-is-too-much-multiple-imputation-mice-r
- https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd - very good explanation for MI with MICE
- http://hsta559s12.pbworks.com/w/file/fetch/52112520/enders.applied
- maybe this helps, too: https://bmcmedresmethodol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12874-017-0442-1

Also, consider to play around with the methods for handling missingness, such as in Tabachnik & Fidell: chapter 4.1.3.5 write about cross-checking different missingness-methods. Maybe, try FIML with estimator = MLR first, even you have categorical data, this could help you to get a feeling of what the results can look like.

I wish you the best.
Marcus

> > > I want to test a multilevel mediation (particularly, test a number of hypotheses about possible mediators of the effect of social class on Right-Wing Authoritarianism) using largely categorical variables surveyed in the General Social Survey, and for this, I would have liked to use Structural Equation Modeling. However, I have doubts about its feasibility, due to missing data.
> > >
> > > In fact, there is not a single participant with data on all variables I want to include, because the items were each asked in different waves or ballots. For example, I would have one item that was only asked in ballots A and B, a second item that only occured in ballots B and C, and a third in ballots A and C. Because I am dealing with categorical data, I am considering WLSMV in Mplus, which uses pairwise deletion. In theory, I can draw up a covariance matrix, since every variable co-occurs with every other variable in one ballot or another: for each pair of variables (so for each covariance I need), I have at least 900 participants (though out of a total of more than 10.000 participants). Therefore, intuitively, using list-wise deletion does not seem very problematic to me, since most missings should be MCAR (they result from randomization in the administration of certain ballots/modules) - with perhaps the exception of a few variables that were not asked in particular years/waves. However, when I read about this, it is often recommended that list-wise deletion is not justified when you have more than 10% missings (a threshold that I far exceed here).
> > >
> > > Is there a method of dealing with missings that allows me to estimate this model, even though each respondent has randomly missing data on around 50% of the variables? Or is it not feasible/advisable to use SEM in my case?
> > >
> > > Thank you in advance for any guidance!

messages.body_plain:
Hey,

"The error messages for the models of the cognitive-behavioral and EMG measures also occur when using only complete cases (cognitive-behavioral: n = 348, EMG: n = 173). I read some common reasons for this problem (e.g. underidentification, missing data, manifest variables have different scales, skewed data), but I think I addressed all these possibilities (I standardized the data, used only complete cases, tried all robust estimators on complete case analysis, and the model should not be underidentified). So if you have an idea, let me know."

Nice to see that you have tried a lot of different options. Have you tried using (a) different marker indicator(s)?
It is very It is very strange that the first two models are not running...

If I got it correctly, you designed a higher order factor model, right?

The approach to assign equal factor loadings seems plausible. You did it via assigning the same label (i. e. "1/3"), my first thought was, this would be kind of a formula to spread the loadings equally among the indicators, but giving a label such as "v1" for each of the indicators of a factor should do the same.
What I would also try, as a sensitivity analyses, would be to play around with the factor loadings; know you assume that they are the same within each of the factors; maybe try to specify different ratios of loading distributions and compare the results. I am not to deep into this, but if your results are stable, than everything should be fine.

Kindly,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: SAM approach with categorical indicators
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jaime,

to my understanding it does make sense, but:

1) Thresholds are indeed in a continuous scale; what you estimate there I assume are tetrachoric (or polychoric if the indicators are polytomic rather than dichotomic) correlations and thresholds, assuming latent utilities (each of the "latent variables" that correspond to each observed variable, for which those thresholds and correlations are computed, which are assumed to be continuous random, normal variables).
2) Meaning "the structural parameters", after applying an estimation method to the measurement model(s) derived from the previous thresholds/correlations.

About your question: It depends on what you mean by "the coefficients". In principle, the interpretation should not differ from the one you would make with any other estimation method within the SEM framework. Maybe I'm not fully getting what you mean, sorry.

In any case, your problem (using the SAM approach with binary items) could be a research question in itself.

Best,
Daniel

--
Daniel Morillo, Ph.D.
GitHub <https://github.com/DaniMori> |  ORCID <https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3021-3878>

messages.subject: Re: model specification second-order
messages.body_plain:
The only part that is (locally) underidentified is the "cognitivebehavioral" latent variable, as it is measured by only two indicators. So you need to add a restriction as you correctly did to one of the parameters, i.e. fixing the loading of AAT_bias_smoking to 1. The rest of the fixed parameters may be adding to many restrictions that the fitted model cannot properly accommodate.

You can try freeing those parameters and leaving only the restriction needed for identification, i.e.:

CFAmodel <- 'cognitivebehavioral =~ 1*AAT_bias_smoking + IAT_app_av_score

             EMG =~ EMGcorr_score + EMGzygo_score + EMGstartle_score
             fMRI =~ ACC + lAG + rThal + rStriatum + lSTG
             sensitization =~ cognitivebehavioral + EMG + fMRI'

Hope that helps!
--
Daniel Morillo, Ph.D.
GitHub <https://github.com/DaniMori> |  ORCID <https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3021-3878>

messages.subject: Re: model specification second-order
messages.body_plain:
Hi Franziska,

The model is correctly specified and should be identified. However, there might be other issues such as small samples size, problems in data processing, severe model misspecification, problems in relationships between manifest variables etc. I suggest you review additional model information such as: size of factor loadings, residuals, distributions and correlations among manifest variables, check if all data were correctly prepared (i.e., no errors in data preparation). This can probably help you identify the issue and try  to remedy it; maybe by dropping some items. In sum, I don't think a precise answer can be given, you need to do a diagnostic check.

Note that your second specification (with some loadings fixed to 1) is not appropriate since you are already setting latent variances to 1 (i.e., "std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE" argument). Either set latent variances to 1 ("std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE") or drop this argument and fix loadings to 1 (although this is what lavaan does by default; if you don't specify std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE of course).

Best,
Jošt

Hi Marcus,

yes, I also tried all possible marker indicators. I guess the reason is that all cognitive-behavioral and all EMG measures do not correlate at all, while all fMRI measures do correlate. So I "force" the cfa function to calculate estimates for a model representing their association, but in data reality, they are not associated at all... On the other hand, this is exactly what we expect, because we think that the theory is not appropriate, at least in our sample.

Yes, from a theoretical point, this model makes most sense (thank you for the hint with the parameters instead of fractions):
CFAmodel_full <- 'cognitivebehavioral =~ a*AAT_bias_smoking + a*IAT_app_av_score + a*IAT_val_score
             EMG =~ b*EMGcorr_score + b*EMGzygo_score + b*EMGstartle_score
             fMRI =~ c*ACC + c*rThal + c*rStriatum + c*lSTG + c*lAG

             sensitization =~ cognitivebehavioral + EMG + fMRI
            '

Thank you very much for your help!
I think I found a "presentable" solution ;)

messages.subject: Seeking Help with Model Non-Identification and Warnings in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Seeking Help with Model Non-Identification and Warnings in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am working on a multigroup SEM using the ESS data from Sweden (2012-2020), and I’ve encountered some persistent issues that I am hoping to get some advice on. The model includes two latent variables representing attitudes towards immigrants and immigration policy, with the former measured by two indicators and the latter by three. After confirming measurement invariance, I introduced demographic (age, gender; categorical variables) and socioeconomic status (education, income; ordinal variables) as formative variables.

The path diagram is as follows.

When fitting the model using WLSMV with ordered categorical variables, I encountered several warnings that I’m struggling to resolve:

Here is the R code and encountered warnings for my model:

M1 <- '
  attitude1 =~ imsmetn + impcntr
  attitude2 =~ imbgeco + imueclt + imwbcnt
  attitude1 ~~ attitude2
  demographic <~ agea + gndr + domicil
  socioeconomic <~ hinctnta + eisced
  attitude1 ~ demographic + socioeconomic
  attitude2 ~ demographic + socioeconomic
'

fit_M1 <- sem(M1, data = swedish_df_age, group = "essround",
              ordered = c("imsmetn", "impcntr", "imbgeco", "imueclt", "imwbcnt"),
              estimator = "WLSMV")

Warning messages:
1: In lav_partable_check(lavpartable, categorical = lavoptions$.categorical,  :
  lavaan WARNING: automatically added intercepts are set to zero:
    [demographic socioeconomic demographic socioeconomic demographic socioeconomic demographic socioeconomic demographic socioeconomic]
2: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.
3: In lav_test_satorra_bentler(lavobject = NULL, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING: could not invert information matrix needed for robust test statistic

I’ve checked for multicollinearity, and re-evaluated my formative indicators. However, these issues persist. I would greatly appreciate any insights or suggestions on:

1.How to properly scale or transform variables to address the variance issue.
2.Approaches to confirming correct model specification for formative indicators.
3.Strategies to ensure model identification and address the issues with the W matrix and information matrix inversion.

Thank you for your time and assistance.

Best regards,
Dinesha Dissanayake

messages.body_plain:
Your attitude1 variable is underidentified, as it only has 2 indicators. Try either of:

setting the two loadings to 1 (the first one is set automatically by default in your syntax):

M1 <- '
  attitude1 =~ imsmetn + 1*impcntr

  attitude2 =~ imbgeco + imueclt + imwbcnt
  attitude1 ~~ attitude2
  demographic <~ agea + gndr + domicil
  socioeconomic <~ hinctnta + eisced
  attitude1 ~ demographic + socioeconomic
  attitude2 ~ demographic + socioeconomic
'

fixing the variance of attitude1:

M1 <- '
  attitude1 =~ imsmetn + impcntr
  attitude2 =~ imbgeco + imueclt + imwbcnt
  attitude1 ~~ attitude2
  demographic <~ agea + gndr + domicil
  socioeconomic <~ hinctnta + eisced
  attitude1 ~ demographic + socioeconomic
  attitude2 ~ demographic + socioeconomic

   attitude1 ~~ 1*attitude1
'
That should at least fix the identification problem.
--
Daniel Morillo, Ph.D.
GitHub <https://github.com/DaniMori> |  ORCID <https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3021-3878>

Hello Dinesha,

have you tried a stepwise approach?
First, I would fit a modell without using the grouping variable, see if that works.
Second, to further explore why your model does not fit, more information are needed (i. e.: sample size, distribution of the variables (maybe zero-inflation problems?),...)
Third, what about first fitting single construct CFAs? Inspect the factor loadings, are they substantial?
Fourth, try a different estimator to see if the model fits in general.

According to the figures you posted, demographic and socioeconomic should not be correlated, maybe insert this restriction into your syntax: demographic ~~ 0*socioeconomic

By the way: what does the following part of the syntax mean? (the <~ statement), have not seen this before, maybe you meant =~?

demographic <~ agea + gndr + domicil
socioeconomic <~ hinctnta + eisced

Hope that helps.
Kindly, Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marcus,

Thank you for your thoughtful suggestions.

In my analysis I use year as the grouping variable and for the first model I consider 5 time points. My first approach was to fit the measurement model with only one endogenous latent variable and 6 indicator variables. Because of the multicollinearity issues I had to remove one variable. Then I fitted another multigroup model with 5 indicators and one latent variable. But RMSEA of that model was higher. Then EFA suggested two factors. So I modified my model to two endogenous latent variables and RMSEA value of the model was below 0.08. Model is as follows.

basic_model <-  'attitude1 =~ imsmetn  + impcntr

                 attitude2 =~ imbgeco + imueclt + imwbcnt

                 attitude1 ~~  attitude2'

I was able to confirm that the model holds measurement invariance. Then I compared latent means and identified the two time points with most noticeable change. My second modeling approach is to assess how latent mean change within those two time periods with the addition of demographic and socioeconomic factors to the model. Now I'm facing warning issues with that model.

I have indeed attempted a stepwise approach, starting without the grouping variable and advancing to a model with a single latent variable. Despite this, the warning messages persist. My initial exploratory factor analysis suggested two factors, which led to the current two-latent-variable model that satisfies measurement invariance with an RMSEA below 0.08.

Regarding your inquiries, the sample size is 7005, and I've ensured the variables are distributed appropriately with no zero-inflation issues. My dataset structure is as follows:

I have also attempted fitting single construct CFAs. However, the standard errors couldn't be computed due to the non-inversion of the information matrix (same warning issues appear).

I appreciate your assistance and am open to any further insights you may have.

In addition to what Marcus suggests, I'd say you may want to check for data missingness and multicollinearity in your variables.

@Marcus the '<-' operator is for defining a latent variable as a formative construct; refer to Dinesha's diagram for the relationships between those variables, you'll see it clearer.

--
Daniel Morillo, Ph.D.

Hi Daniel,

I did check for missing data and multicollinearity at the beginning of my analysis. To address missing values I used listwise deletion. Regarding multicollinearity, I identified and removed one out of six indicators due to a high correlation with the other two variables, which explains why I currently have only two indicators per latent variable for attitudes towards immigrants.

Your insights are much appreciated.

Best,
Dinesha Dissanayake

messages.subject: Unspecified model in measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
Good morning,

After testing a model in CFA (Mod.6) which I copy below, it gives me a marginal adjustment, but the model is well specified without negative variances and without values more than 1. I present a model after an EFA (in a different split sample) (Mod.1) which in the measurement invariance (EFA sample + CFA sample) is correctly specified. Model 6 is a theoretical model. This model consists of a pain factor, a hyperreactivity factor (with two factors and corresponding items) and a hyperreactivity factor (with three factors and corresponding items). I have tested a second-order model to see if a single instrument score can be used, the ouput of r is OK. However, when I want to perform a measurement invariance according to the sex of Mod.6 in the total sample, I get a warning in r that the model is not well specified. What could be happening, can someone help me?

Thanks in advance

Néstor Montoro-Pérez
Alicante University

messages.subject: Re: RI-CLPM within-centered variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ryan,

Thank you, I looked at the paper again and it is helpful.

If I understand correctly a RI-CLPM differs from a CLPM by addition as both the within-centered variables as the between-centered variables (the RI).

My code for the RI-CLPM is this with the variables diet (DHD) and depression (EPDS) at 3 waves (18 weeks of pregnancy, 32 weeks of pregnancy and 12 weeks postpartum)

RICLPM1 <- '
# Create between components (random intercepts)
RIx =~ 1*EPDS_pre_18_win_sqr + 1*EPDS_pre_32_win_sqr + 1*EPDS_post_12_win_sqr
RIy =~ 1*DHD_total_pre_18s + 1*DHD_total_pre_32s + 1*DHD_total_post_12_wins

# Create within-person centered variables

EPDS1 =~ 1*EPDS_pre_18_win_sqr
EPDS2 =~ 1*EPDS_pre_32_win_sqr
EPDS3 =~ 1*EPDS_post_12_win_sqr
DHD1 =~ 1*DHD_total_pre_18s
DHD2 =~ 1*DHD_total_pre_32s
DHD3 =~1*DHD_total_post_12_wins

# Estimate lagged effects between within-person centered variables
EPDS2 ~ EPDS1 + DHD1
EPDS3 ~ EPDS2 + DHD2
DHD2 ~ DHD1 + EPDS1
DHD3 ~ DHD2 + EPDS2

# Estimate covariance between within-person centered variables at first wave
EPDS1 ~~ DHD1 # Covariance

# Estimate covariances between residuals of within-person centered variables
# (i.e., innovations)
EPDS2 ~~ DHD2
EPDS3 ~~ DHD3

# Estimate variance and covariance of random intercepts
RIx ~~ RIx
RIy ~~ RIy
RIx ~~ RIy

# Estimate (residual) variance of within-person centered variables
EPDS1 ~~ EPDS1 # Variances
DHD1 ~~ DHD1
EPDS2 ~~ EPDS2 # Residual variances
DHD2 ~~ DHD2
EPDS3 ~~ EPDS3
DHD3 ~~ DHD3
'
# fit the model to the data
fit1 <- sem(RICLPM1, missing = "ML",data = df)

# view the model results
summary(fit1, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE,  ci = TRUE)

I get these warnings, which indicates this code cannot run on our data, maybe because our sample is too small (N=160 wave 1, N=150 wave 2 and N=145 wave 3):

In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats, :

lavaan WARNING: Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not identified. In lav_object_post_check(object)

lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative

The model for the traditional CLPM is quite simplified and does run and I used this code instead:

CLPM1c <- '

# Estimate lagged effects

EPDS_pre_32_win_sqr  ~ EPDS_pre_18_win_sqr + DHD_total_pre_18s

EPDS_post_12_win_sqr ~ EPDS_pre_32_win_sqr  + DHD_total_pre_32s

DHD_total_pre_32s ~ DHD_total_pre_18s+ EPDS_pre_18_win_sqr

DHD_total_post_12_wins ~ DHD_total_pre_32s + EPDS_pre_32_win_sqr

# Estimate covariances

EPDS_pre_18_win_sqr ~~ DHD_total_pre_18s# Covariance

EPDS_pre_32_win_sqr  ~~ DHD_total_pre_32s

EPDS_post_12_win_sqr ~~ DHD_total_post_12_wins

'

# fit the model to the data

fit1c <- sem(CLPM1c, missing = "ML", data = df)

# view the model results

summary(fit1c, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE,  ci = TRUE)

Is it now best to simplify the models by using the second code and just go on with a traditional CLPM, without the random intercepts and within-centered variables? Or could I add something to this code to keep in mind also within-person change, but still make my model run?

Thank you for your help!!

Kind regards,

Nina

messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel and  Marcus  ,

I truly appreciate your willingness to help. Based on your advices, I revisited the model specification. Interestingly, transforming formative indicators to reflective ones allowed the model to fit without the non-computing standard errors/ non-inversion of the information matrix issue.  However,  using the WLSMV estimator (all variables in my dataset is ordinal/ categorical variables with less than 6 levels) resulted in a following non-convergence warning:

Warning message:
In lavaan::lavaan(model = M1, data = swedish_df_age, ordered = TRUE,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    the optimizer warns that a solution has NOT been found!

Subsequently, when I applied the ML estimator, the model converged without any issues. Yet, due to concerns about not assuming normality, I tested both MLR and MLM estimators. They also fit the model well but flagged an issue:

Warning message:

In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:

    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
    (= -6.064597e-22) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that

    the model is not identified.

Given the data's ordinal nature, what would you suggest is the best estimator to use in this scenario? Should I be concerned about the warning regarding the variance-covariance matrix when using MLR and MLM estimators?

Thank you once again for your valuable input.

Warm regards,
Dinesha Dissanayake

messages.subject: Re: RI-CLPM within-centered variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nina,

I think the issue might be that you are using the “sem” function to run the model. Try using “lavaan” instead, so fit1 <- lavaan(RICLPM1, missing = “ML”, data - df). The “sem” function is a wrapper function that has several built-in defaults that do not work for the RI-CLPM, which I believe is causing the warning message you are receiving about the model possibly not being identified. The “lavaan” function is “default-light” and should be able to run the model you are trying to estimate.

Best,

Ryan

> If I understand correctly a RI-CLPM differs from a CLPM by addition as both the within-centered variables as the between-centered variables (the RI).
>
>
>
> My code for the RI-CLPM is this with the variables diet (DHD) and depression (EPDS) at 3 waves (18 weeks of pregnancy, 32 weeks of pregnancy and 12 weeks postpartum)
>
> RICLPM1 <- '
> # Create between components (random intercepts)
> RIx =~ 1*EPDS_pre_18_win_sqr + 1*EPDS_pre_32_win_sqr + 1*EPDS_post_12_win_sqr
> RIy =~ 1*DHD_total_pre_18s + 1*DHD_total_pre_32s + 1*DHD_total_post_12_wins
>
>
> # Create within-person centered variables
>
> EPDS1 =~ 1*EPDS_pre_18_win_sqr
> EPDS2 =~ 1*EPDS_pre_32_win_sqr
> EPDS3 =~ 1*EPDS_post_12_win_sqr
> DHD1 =~ 1*DHD_total_pre_18s
> DHD2 =~ 1*DHD_total_pre_32s
> DHD3 =~1*DHD_total_post_12_wins
>
> # Estimate lagged effects between within-person centered variables
> EPDS2 ~ EPDS1 + DHD1
> EPDS3 ~ EPDS2 + DHD2
> DHD2 ~ DHD1 + EPDS1
> DHD3 ~ DHD2 + EPDS2
>
> # Estimate covariance between within-person centered variables at first wave
> EPDS1 ~~ DHD1 # Covariance
>
> # Estimate covariances between residuals of within-person centered variables
> # (i.e., innovations)
> EPDS2 ~~ DHD2
> EPDS3 ~~ DHD3
>
> # Estimate variance and covariance of random intercepts
> RIx ~~ RIx
> RIy ~~ RIy
> RIx ~~ RIy
>
> # Estimate (residual) variance of within-person centered variables
> EPDS1 ~~ EPDS1 # Variances
> DHD1 ~~ DHD1
> EPDS2 ~~ EPDS2 # Residual variances
> DHD2 ~~ DHD2
> EPDS3 ~~ EPDS3
> DHD3 ~~ DHD3
> '
> # fit the model to the data

> lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative
>
>
>
> The model for the traditional CLPM is quite simplified and does run and I used this code instead:
>
> CLPM1c <- '
>
> # Estimate lagged effects
>
> EPDS_pre_32_win_sqr  ~ EPDS_pre_18_win_sqr + DHD_total_pre_18s
>
> EPDS_post_12_win_sqr ~ EPDS_pre_32_win_sqr  + DHD_total_pre_32s
>
> DHD_total_pre_32s ~ DHD_total_pre_18s+ EPDS_pre_18_win_sqr
>
> DHD_total_post_12_wins ~ DHD_total_pre_32s + EPDS_pre_32_win_sqr
>
> # Estimate covariances
>
> EPDS_pre_18_win_sqr ~~ DHD_total_pre_18s# Covariance
>
> EPDS_pre_32_win_sqr  ~~ DHD_total_pre_32s
>
> EPDS_post_12_win_sqr ~~ DHD_total_post_12_wins
>
> '
>
> # fit the model to the data
>
> fit1c <- sem(CLPM1c, missing = "ML", data = df)
>
> # view the model results
>
> summary(fit1c, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE,  ci = TRUE)
>
> Is it now best to simplify the models by using the second code and just go on with a traditional CLPM, without the random intercepts and within-centered variables? Or could I add something to this code to keep in mind also within-person change, but still make my model run?
>
> Thank you for your help!!
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear Dinesha,

fine. You should not worry much about the warning as Terence wrote here:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/4y5pmqRz4nk

Concerning the estimator: have you tried other estimators? https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/est.html? There is big discussion which estimator is best, a google search maybe helps here. In the context of structural equation modeling with ordinal data, the MLR (Robust Maximum Likelihood) and WLSMV (Weighted Least Squares with Means and Variances adjusted) estimators have proven to be practicable (see Li, 2016, p. 939).
I think you can try comparing both estimators. Why the model with the wlsmv does not fit is beyond my understanding. Have you played a bit with the settings?

Kindly,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

For the higher-order CFA model below, my understanding is that std.lv <http://std.lv> fixes the variances of the (exogenous) second-order factors cost1 and cost2 to 1 and fixes the residual variances of the (endogenous) first-order factors TE, OE, LV, and EM to 1.

mod <- "TE    =~ TE1 + TE2 + TE3 + TE4 + TE5
        OE    =~ OE1 + OE2 + OE3 + OE4
        LV    =~ LVA1 + LVA2 + LVA3 + LVA4
        EM    =~ EM1 + EM2 + EM3 + EM4 + EM5 + EM6
        cost1 =~ TE + OE
        cost2 =~ LV + EM"

fit <- cfa(mod, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ml")
summary(fit, standardized = TRUE)

I have a couple questions about this:

1. I can see in the "Estimate" column of the summary that the residual variances in addition to the variances are fixed to 1 (in yellow). messages.subject: Re: Unspecified model in measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Néstor.

As the message indicates, the real problem is that a covariance matrix is not positive-definite.
One common reason is that the model is not identified, but there may be other ones, like small sample size or high number of missing data.

Remember that in Mod.1 and Mod.6, a single matrix is constructed based on the whole sample. When testing invariance, one matrix is constructed for each group. Thus, I recommend you to check the sexes separately to see which one is causing the error.

Best regards,
Yago

messages.subject: Simulating SEM data
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to create simulated datasets to test the differences that occur under different model structures. I'm using simsem in R to do this and have had no luck getting it to actually simulate the datasets successfully. I need to generate datasets that have nine indicators (x1 - x9) used to measure a multidimensional latent variable (D) that has three dimensions (A, B, C). Factor A is measured by x1, x2, x3. Factor B is measured by x4, x5, x6.  Factor C is measured by x7, x8, x9. Y is regressed on D. The lower-order factor loadings should all be set to .4, the higher-order factor loadings should all be set to .5, and the strength of the path coefficient between D --> Y should be set to .25, all as shown below. I also want to calculate three parcels in the datasets, each calculated based on the averages specified in the measurement portion of the model below. I've been using the following syntax:

# Load packages
library(simsem)
library(lavaan)

set.seed(12345)

# Sim data model
simModel <- '
  # Measurement
  A =~ 0.4*x1 + 0.4*x2 + 0.4*x3
  B =~ 0.4*x4 + 0.4*x5 + 0.4*x6
  C =~ 0.4*x7 + 0.4*x8 + 0.4*x9

  # Parcels
  P123 = (x1 + x2 + x3)/3
  P456 = (x4 + x5 + x6)/3
  P789 = (x7 + x8 + x9)/3

  # Structural
  D =~ 0.5*A + 0.5*B + 0.5*C
  Y ~ 0.25*D

  # Variances
  A ~~ 0.75*A
  B ~~ 0.75*B
  C ~~ 0.75*C
  '

# Homogeneous fit model
fit_hom <- '
  # Measures
  A =~ P123
  B =~ P456
  C =~ P789
  D =~ A + B + C

  Y ~ D
  '

# Run simulation with N = 500
simOutput_1 <- sim(
  nRep = 1500,
  model = fit_hom,
  n = 500,
  generate = simModel,
  lavaanfun = 'lavaan',
  se = 'standard'
)

When I run the above, it tells me:
Progress: 1 / 1500 Error in str2lang(x) : <text>:1:40: unexpected symbol 1: ~ 0.4*x7+0.4*x8+0.4*x9P123=(x1+x2+x3)/3P456

I am having trouble determining what is going wrong. I suspect I am goofing something up in the simModel or have omitted something critical in my fitModel, but I am not certain. Any insight from anyone that could help me troubleshoot this so that I can get it to work successfully would be extremely appreciated. This is my first time doing this, so it would be so helpful. Thank you!

messages.body_plain:
Hey Dinesha,

great. Consider coding your dichotomous variables always 0/1! Does it fit now?

Can't imagine why there were problems, maybe because each of these 3 variables of the factor has a different metric? If you want to keep gender as a variable, you could z-standardize all variables within this factor and then take these variables into the CFA, maybe then it will work.

Concerning the choice of the estimators: please, search in academic databases concerning this issue, there should be simulation studies. Try out search terms such as: estimator choice categorical variables ... .I really like the MLR because you can use FIML - virtually the best choice when you have missing data --> try it out, because listwise deletion is only pragmatic but not a good choice in dealing with missingness.

Kindly,
Marcus

messages.subject: Binary exogenous categorical variable in growth model factor vs numeric
messages.subject_clean: Binary exogenous categorical variable in growth model factor vs numeric
messages.body_plain:
Dear all, I run a growth model with an exogenous categorical variable (cat) coded 0/1 and get different values for my fitmeasures (cfi, tli,rmsea, chisq) when it is coded as a factor and a numeric variable. I receive no errors from Lavaan while running the model.
Do anyone know why this happens, and what format would be correct?

For context:
growth_model <-
  '
i1 =~ 1*ytime1 + 1*ytime2 + 1*ytime3
s1 =~ 0*ytime1 + 1.5*ytime2 + 3.5*ytime3
ytime1 ~~ ytime1
ytime2 ~~ ytime2
ytime3 ~~ ytime3
i1 ~~ i1
s1 ~~ s1
i1 ~~ s1
ytime1 ~ 0*1 + cat
ytime2 ~ 0*1 + cat
ytime3 ~ 0*1 + cat
i1 ~ 1
s1 ~ 1
'
model<-growth(growth_model, data=df)
fitMeasures(model)

messages.subject: Re: Simulating SEM data
messages.body_plain:
I am not familiar with simsem::sim(). I did a quick check and I think you can try the following suggestions:

- Remove these lines from simModel. They are not valid model syntax lines. They led to the error you encountered.

  P123 = (x1 + x2 + x3)/3
  P456 = (x4 + x5 + x6)/3
  P789 = (x7 + x8 + x9)/3

- If you want to create parcels on the generated dataframe, write a function that has this form, and pass it to the datafun argument of sim():

create_parcels <- function(dat_i) {
  # dat_i is the data generated form simModel
  # Create parcels
  # Return a dataframe with the parcels.
}

The call should be something like this:

simOutput_1 <- sim(
 ...
 datafun = create_parcels,
 ...
)

- Something's wrong with fit_hom. A, B, and C are one-indicator factors. Is this what you want?

  D =~ P123 + P456 + P789

To check fit_hom, you can test it using only one dataset first:

data_test <- simulateData(simModel,
                          sample.nobs = 500,
                          seed = 1234)
fit <- sem(fit_hom, data = data_test)

Revise fit_hom until it works as expected for one dataset. You can then call sim().

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject: Re: Binary exogenous categorical variable in growth model factor vs numeric
messages.subject_clean: Binary exogenous categorical variable in growth model factor vs numeric
messages.body_plain:
I believe your model is not invariant to the scaling of cat. When coded as a factor, the values are 1 and 2, which are used directly by lavaan.

You can try changing the numneric coding of cat to 1 and 2. I believe the fit measures willl be identical to those with cat coded as a factor.

You can also try changing the values of cat to, say, 2 and 3. I believe you will get another set of fit measures.

You may need to check your model specification.

-- Shu Fai

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nina,

It is definitely possible that the RI-CLPM is not the most appropriate model for the data you have. That said, I would recommend you inspect the parameter estimates in your output to see if there is anything that looks off. That could signal the model is doing something you don't want or intend, and you should modify your syntax. Another check is to request modification indices (i.e., modindices; https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/modindices.html). This is a data-driven way to see if there is something not estimated in the model that "should" be estimated. Lots of people have lots of different opinions about modification indices, but from a purely diagnostic standpoint, I think they can help you catch unintended omissions.

Best,

Ryan

Hi,

cat(specmod) should print the model, not the data. But looking at the printout of your data, the variable names are

variables        X2022        X2021        X2020        X2019           X2018

This means that your data are in an incorrect format and you need to reshape or pivot the data.

https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-tidy.html#sec-pivoting

That being said, I strongly recommend starting with just a set of two regressions (lm command) to estimate your model. Once you have that working, you can move to more advanced analyses.

Mikko

messages.subject_clean: Negative chi-square and df in EFA with PML-AC estimation
messages.body_plain:
Hi, everyone,

I ran EFAs for 36 ordinal items (each on a 4-point Likert scale) with 2-6 factors using pairwise maximum likelihood estimation ("PML") on available cases ("available.cases").

efa(nfactors = 2:6, rotation = "oblimin", ordered = TRUE, estimator = "PML", missing = "available.cases")

It seems odd in the summary that except for the case of 3 factors, the chi-square and degrees of freedom are negative. Any idea what might be going on?

The full summary output is attached. I would very much appreciate any input!

Jeremy

Thank you very much Dr Rosseel

El viernes, 12 de abril de 2024 a las 8:13:36 UTC-5, yros...@gmail.com escribió:
> Hello Jaime,
>
> I can confirm that the SAM approach works with categorical indicators.
> The interpretation of the coefficients does not change: they are on the
> same scale as if you would have used the sem() function.
>
> Yves.
>
> On 4/3/24 10:46 PM, 'JAIME ANDRES GAVIRIA BEDOYA' via lavaan wrote:
> > Hi everyone.
> >
> > I'm a phd student.
> >
> > After reading again the Rossel and Loh paper (2022) about sam approach I
> > realized it was developed assuming continuous and latent variable
> > indicators. So, I was thinking if this approach would make sense in case
> > my items are categorical:
> >
> > 1) To run a sem model with binary items with their corresponding
> > thresholds, which indeed are assumed to be continuous.
> > 2) Then, estimate the parameters with the sam approach.
> >
> > The issue I found is about the interpretation of the coefficients. Any
> > suggestions?
> >
> >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marcus,

Thank you for your suggestions. I tried coding the dichotomous gender variables as 0/1 and also z-standardizing all variables within the latent factor that includes the gender variable. Unfortunately, neither method resolved the issue. Considering this, I am thinking of removing the gender variable or proceeding with the MLR estimator.

Thank you again for your guidance.

Kind regards,
Dinesha

>
> Concerning the choice of the estimators: please, search in academic databases concerning this issue, there should be simulation studies. Try out search terms such as: estimator choice categorical variables ... .I really like the MLR because you can use FIML - virtually the best choice when you have missing data --> try it out, because listwise deletion is only pragmatic but not a good choice in dealing with missingness.

messages.body_plain:
Hi. So I am trying to use the runMI() function of the semTools package to fit a multiple impute ordinal MG-CFA model. However, it seems like R isn't finding the correct summary() methods for lavaan.mi-class objects, instead using the method for lavaanList-class objects, as per this discussion <https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/Kjsb1v2nd2s>. My code looks like this (also attached):

```{r}
rm(list=ls()) # Clean workspace
options(scipen=10000) # Set scientific notation
library(tidyverse)
library(lavaan) # For CFA
library(semTools) # For measurement of invariance in MGCFA
set.seed(121012) # For reproducibility

# Create simulated categorical dataset with missing values
popModel <- "
f1 =~ 0.6*y1 + 0.6*y2 + 0.6*y3 + 0.6*y4
y1 ~*~ 1*y1
y2 ~*~ 1*y2
y3 ~*~ 1*y3
y4 ~*~ 1*y4
f1 ~~ 1*f1
y1 | 0.5*t1
y2 | 0.25*t1
y3 | 0*t1
y4 | -0.5*t1
"

dat <- simulateData(popModel, sample.nobs  = 200L)
miss.pat <- matrix(as.logical(rbinom(prod(dim(dat)), 1, 0.2)), nrow(dat), ncol(dat))
dat[miss.pat] <- NA

# Convert columns to factors with specified levels
dat$y1 <- factor(dat$y1, levels = c(1, 2))
dat$y2 <- factor(dat$y2, levels = c(1, 2))
dat$y3 <- factor(dat$y3, levels = c(1, 2))
dat$y4 <- factor(dat$y4, levels = c(1, 2))

# Define categories for a grouping variable school
schools <- c("Marx", "Durkheim", "Weber", "Comte")

# Sample the school categories randomly for each row
dat$school <- sample(schools, size = nrow(dat), replace = TRUE)

# Define Ordinal MG-CFA model
analyzeModel <- "
f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
y1 ~*~ 1*y1
y2 ~*~ 1*y2
y3 ~*~ 1*y3
y4 ~*~ 1*y4
"
# Create predictor matrix
predictormatrix<-quickpred(dat)

# Impute 5 datasets (common practice)
dat_imp <- mice(data = dat,
                           predictorMatrix = predictormatrix,
                           m = 5,
                           # Specify imputation method for ordinal data
                           method = "polr")

mice.imp <- NULL
for(i in 1:5) mice.imp[[i]] <- complete(dat_imp, action=i, inc=FALSE)

# run lavaan with previously imputed data using runMI
out2 <- semTools::runMI(analyzeModel,
                        data = mice.imp,
                        fun = "cfa",
                        meanstructure = TRUE,
                        group = "school", ordered = TRUE,
                        std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

detach("package:tidyverse", unload = TRUE)
library(semTools)

summary(out2)
```

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I plan to run a local SAM model using the sam() function in lavaan. I tried this out using Example 1 of the Rosseel & Loh (2022) paper  <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36355708/>(the dataset and script can be found here <https://osf.io/pekbm/>). This works fine, but for my own research, I will have categorical indicators (mostly Likert items, some dichotomous items). I recently saw here <https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/zbmR2e4yGsc/m/DisSOVKSAQAJ> that sam() now also works with categorical indicators, which is great.

I tried whether this works by declaring the indicator variables of the example dataset as ordered factors, and running the following model:

model <- '
  # measurement part
    ost   =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
    self  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
    other =~ x4 + x5 + x6
  # structural part
    ost   ~ b1*self + b2*other + c*sol + age + gender
    self  ~ a1*sol + age + gender
    other ~ a2*sol + age + gender
  # residual correlations
    self ~~ other '

fit.lsam_o2 <- sam(model, data = Data2, sam.method = "local", ordered = c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x4", "x5", "x6", "y1", "y2", "y3", "y4"))

When I run this model, I get the following warnings:

Warning messages:
1: In sam(model, data = Data2, sam.method = "local", ordered = c("x1",  :
  lavaan WARNING: sam() does not support conditional.x = TRUE (yet)
  -> switching to conditional.x = FALSE
2: In muthen1984(Data = X[[g]], wt = WT[[g]], ov.names = ov.names[[g]],  :
  lavaan WARNING: trouble constructing W matrix; used generalized inverse for A11 submatrix

I am struggling to understand what these warnings mean, and what the implications are for my analyses (i.e., is this a problem?). If anyone could help me out, that would be extremely helpful.

Re Warning 1: Here  <https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/EWqFQO3FZds/m/1vwLzmb-AAAJ>I read a more technical explanation about what conditional.x = FALSE means. I have to admit I have not been able to wrap my head around whether this would be problematic, or not. Are there situations were this would be problematic?
I also read this here: <https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/lavaan/html/lavOptions.html> "By default, in the categorical case we use conditional.x = TRUE. Therefore, any cases with missing values on the exogenous covariates will be deleted listwise from the data first." I can see how that would be problematic in case of missing values. I do have missing values, but I plan to use multiple imputation to create multiple complete datasets, so I think this should not be an issue.

Re Warning 2: Here  <https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/6SiW_hhCOmg/m/uZHbh-WVBQAJ>is a post that concerns that same warning, and which seems to state that if you want to use WLSMV as estimator (which I do), conditional.x needs  to be TRUE, otherwise something goes wrong in the estimation stage. However, this seems to contradict Yves Rosseel's (more recent) statement <https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/zbmR2e4yGsc/m/DisSOVKSAQAJ> that sam() now also works for categorical variables. Does anyone know more about this, or about Warning 2 in general?

Thanks very much!

Best,
Floor

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to set up a mediated moderation model in lavaan.

It seems trickier than I first anticipated. And the advice available around it appears pretty variable (e.g. in terms of syntax).

I would be hugely appreciative if I could get some feedback on my syntax.

I am interested in plotting simple slopes at several quantiles for Moderator1, and Moderator2 is just a binary coded variable (male/female).

I scaled all of the data prior to running the model (centered, scaled), and created interaction terms prior to feeding into lavaan (i.e. interaction between MEDIATOR and Moderator1 is MEDIATOR_X_Moderator1)

I was attempting to follow the following code:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/doiIqqVc5TY/m/ndSXbDIuBAAJ

https://gist.github.com/TomTrebs/15b84bb7d09dcf7f4a25201b9ca66629

https://ademos.people.uic.edu/Chapter15.html#5_moderated_mediation_analyses_using_%E2%80%9Clavaan%E2%80%9D_package

I have attached an image of what I want to test.

#My syntax:

#Mediated Moderation

Y ~ b1*MEDIATOR + b2*MEDIATOR_X_Moderator1 + b3*MEDIATOR_X_Moderator2 + control1 + Control2+ cprime1*Predictor + Moderator2 + Moderator1 + cprime2*Predictor_X_Moderator1 + cprime3*Predictor_X_Moderator2 +Control3 + Control4+Control5+ Control6+ Control7

MEDIATOR ~ a1*Predictor + Moderator2 + Moderator1 + a2*Predictor_X_Moderator1 + a3*Predictor_X_Moderator2 + Control3 + Control4 + Control2+ control1+Control5+ Control6+ Control7

#Allow residuals to correlate between interactions and original vars

MEDIATOR~~MEDIATOR_X_Moderator1 +MEDIATOR_X_Moderator2

MEDIATOR_X_Moderator1 ~~MEDIATOR_X_Moderator2

Predictor ~~Predictor_X_Moderator1 +Predictor_X_Moderator2

Predictor_X_Moderator1 ~~Predictor_X_Moderator2

Moderator2 ~~MEDIATOR_X_Moderator2 +Predictor_X_Moderator2

Moderator1 ~~MEDIATOR_X_Moderator1 +Predictor_X_Moderator1

MEDIATOR_X_Moderator1 ~~Predictor_X_Moderator1

MEDIATOR_X_Moderator2 ~~Predictor_X_Moderator2

#Simple slope of Mediator (M) on X (predictor) at quantiles of Moderator 1

SS_MxX_Q1 := a1+a2*(-0.91555474209508)

SS_MxX_Q2 := a1+a2*(-0.91555474209508)

SS_MxX_Q3 := a1+a2*(-0.326983836462529)

SS_MxX_Q4 := a1+a2*(0.653967672925057)

SS_MxX_Q5 := a1+a2*(1.32101469930862)

SS_MxX_NoMod := a1+a2*(0)

#Simple slope of Mediator on X at levels of Moderator 2

SS_MxX_Moderator2Male := a1+a3*(-2.01303598658837)

SS_MxX_Moderator2Female := a1+a3*(0.494429891442757)

SS_MxX_Moderator2_NoMod := a1+a3*(0)

#Simple slope of Y (outcome) on M (mediator) at quantiles of Moderator 1

SS_YxM_Q1 := b1+b2*(-0.91555474209508)

SS_YxM_Q2 := b1+b2*(-0.91555474209508)

SS_YxM_Q3 := b1+b2*(-0.326983836462529)

SS_YxM_Q4 := b1+b2*(0.653967672925057)

SS_YxM_Q5 := b1+b2*(1.32101469930862)

SS_YxM_NoMod := b1+b2*(0)

#Simple slope of Y on X at levels of Moderator 2

SS_YxM_Moderator2Male := b1+b3*(-2.01303598658837)

SS_YxM_Moderator2Female := b1+b3*(0.494429891442757)

SS_YxM_Moderator2_NoMod := b1+b3*(0)

#Indirect effects conditional on moderators

IE_cond_Q1 := SS_MxX_Q1*SS_YxM_Q1

IE_cond_Q2 := SS_MxX_Q2*SS_YxM_Q2

IE_cond_Q3 := SS_MxX_Q3*SS_YxM_Q3

IE_cond_Q4 := SS_MxX_Q4*SS_YxM_Q4

IE_cond_Q5 := SS_MxX_Q5*SS_YxM_Q5

IE_cond_NoMod := SS_MxX_NoMod*SS_YxM_NoMod

IE_cond_Moderator2Male := SS_MxX_Moderator2Male*SS_YxM_Moderator2Male

IE_cond_Moderator2Female := SS_MxX_Moderator2Female*SS_YxM_Moderator2Female

IE_cond_Moderator2_NoMod := SS_MxX_Moderator2_NoMod*SS_YxM_Moderator2_NoMod

#Direct effects conditional on moderator 1

DE_cond_Q1 := cprime1+cprime2*(-0.91555474209508)

DE_cond_Q2 := cprime1+cprime2*(-0.91555474209508)

DE_cond_Q3 := cprime1+cprime2*(-0.326983836462529)

DE_cond_Q4 := cprime1+cprime2*(0.653967672925057)

DE_cond_Q5 := cprime1+cprime2*(1.32101469930862)

DE_cond_NoMod := cprime1+cprime2*(0)

#Direct effects conditional on moderator 2

DE_cond_Moderator2Male := cprime1+cprime3*(-2.01303598658837)

DE_cond_Moderator2Female := cprime1+cprime3*(0.494429891442757)

DE_cond_Moderator2_NoMod := cprime1+cprime3*(0)

#Total effects conditional on moderator 1

total.Q1 := DE_cond_Q1 + IE_cond_Q1

total.Q2 := DE_cond_Q2 + IE_cond_Q2

total.Q3 := DE_cond_Q3 + IE_cond_Q3

total.Q4 := DE_cond_Q4 + IE_cond_Q4

total.Q5 := DE_cond_Q5 + IE_cond_Q5

total.NoMod := DE_cond_NoMod + IE_cond_NoMod

#Total effects conditional on moderator 2

total.Moderator2Male := DE_cond_Moderator2Male + IE_cond_Moderator2Male

total.Moderator2Female := DE_cond_Moderator2Female + IE_cond_Moderator2Female

total.Moderator2_NoMod := DE_cond_Moderator2_NoMod + IE_cond_Moderator2_NoMod

#Proportion mediated

propmediated.Q1 := IE_cond_Q1 / total.Q1

propmediated.Q2 := IE_cond_Q2 / total.Q2

propmediated.Q3 := IE_cond_Q3 / total.Q3

propmediated.Q4 := IE_cond_Q4 / total.Q4

propmediated.Q5 := IE_cond_Q5 / total.Q5

propmediated.NoMod := IE_cond_NoMod / total.NoMod

propmediated.Moderator2Male := IE_cond_Moderator2Male / total.Moderator2Male

propmediated.Moderator2Female := IE_cond_Moderator2Female / total.Moderator2Female

propmediated.Moderator2Female := IE_cond_Moderator2_NoMod / total.Moderator2_NoMod

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nina,

The modification index is suggesting that you estimate the mean, or intercept, of RIx. I have one additional idea to try out. When you estimate the model, add meanstructure = TRUE and int.ov.free=TRUE. Together, these commands will bring the intercepts of the observed variables into the model and freely estimate them. I believe this is what is missing from the syntax, and it is why the modification indices are suggesting that you estimate the mean of RIx. So, your call would now look like:

fit1 <- lavaan(RICLPM1, missing = “ML”, data = df, meanstructure = TRUE, int.ov.free = TRUE)

Best,

Ryan

messages.subject: Re: Questions about intercept
messages.body_plain:
Dear Erwan,

For 1), I don't know how to give you an exact technical explanation, but more or less I would say that the estimation of the covariance structure is independent of the estimation of the mean structure.

For 2), you are increasing the number of parameter estimates by 5 (the 5 intercepts), but you are also increasing the number of "data points" you use to estimate the model, by using the (5) means of your observable variables. You can run the computations like this:

Without mean structure:
Nº of data values: 5 variances + 10 covariances = 15
Nº of parameters: 4 loadings + 5 unique variances + 1 latent variance = 10
DoF: 15 - 10 = 5

With mean structure:
Nº of data values: 5 variances + 10 covariances + 5 means = 20
Nº of parameters: 4 factor loadings + 5 unique variances + 1 latent variance + 5 intercepts = 15
DoF: 20 - 15 = 5

Hope it helps!

--
Daniel Morillo, Ph.D.

messages.subject: Re: Questions about intercept
messages.body_plain:
Daniel's explanation is entirely correct, but I want to expand just a bit. Part of the issue with fit not changing is that the mean structure model is saturated. You have 5 observed means as data points, and you estimate 5 mean structure parameters, the intercepts. A saturated model does not contribute to lack of fit. Your covariance structure model is not saturated, so if you estimated only mean structure first and then added covariance structure, you would see a change in fit.
     The maximum likelihood discrepancy function for a mean and covariance structure model includes two parts, one part for the covariance structure and one part for the mean structure. There is no interaction term. Few models entangle the two together, although ones that do so, ironically, are latent interaction models. One could also imagine some multiple group analyses creating the potential for the two parts of the model to interact, such that certain forms of misspecification of mean structure might lead to bias in estimation of some covariance structure parameters.
     I believe the lavaan package functions do not automatically estimate mean structure parameters unless your model syntax explicitly mentions a mean structure parameter. But check your output to be sure. Yes, it is unnerving when the number of parameters estimated changes but degrees of freedom do not. Maybe the software needs to break down parameters estimated and degrees of freedom by mean structure vs covariance structure.

messages.subject: Re: Variance decomposition using sequential mediation
messages.body_plain:
I don't think you can use relaimpo, detached from a correlation matrix. These methods (pmvd, lmg. ...) are somewhat exclusive for multiple regressions and not for mediation. I guess there are 2 options: Upsilon (Lachowitz et al) or Delta Med.Liu et al). I wouldn't buy the latter. My 2 Cents.

HTH

Christian

> Dear whom it may concern,
>
> I would sincerely appreciate any suggestions on this topic. I think my essential goal is to partition the marginal R^2 for each predictor, after accounting for mediating effects.
>
> I am aware of packages like misty, relaimpo to generate the indices of my interest based on correlation matrices. So, my question would become, what is the proper way to have a correlation matrix of all factors, after accounting for mediating paths? I tried lavInspect(fit, "cor.all"), which gave me all the same no matter how many mediating paths I added. I reckon there must be mistakes. Any suggestions will be appreciated.
>
> Best wishes,
> Y
>
> On Monday 29 April 2024 at 17:24:15 UTC+1 Yira Zhang wrote:
> > Dear all,
> >
> > I am using sequential mediation analyses (aka serial mediation) in lavaan in R.
> >
> > Below is my model
> > ```
> > model <- "y ~ a*x1 + b*x2 + c*x3 + d*x4
> > x1 ~ b1*x2 + c2*x3 + d2*x4
> > x2 ~ c3*x3 + d3*x4
> >
> > x2_y := b1*a + b
> > x3_y := c2*a + c3*b + c
> > x4_y := d2*a + d3*b + d
> > "
> >
> > fit <- sem(model)
> > ```
> >
> > I would like to conduct something like dominance analysis to decompose the variance explained of the outcome variable, similar to R^2 of each predictor in linear multiple regression.
> >
> > For the baseline regression model, I now know a function which can give my intended results:
> > ```
> > model_baseline <- "
> > y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4"
> > fit_baseline <- sem(model_baseline)
> > fit_baseline.cor <- lavCor(fit_baseline)
> > misty::dominance.manual(fit_baseline.cor)
> > ```
> > My question is regarding when adding more mediation paths, how can I get the variance explained by each factor? Potentially lower values for mediators and higher values for factors being mediated. Any suggestions upon packages, functions, or manual calculations would be appreciated.
> >
> > I know my model is not exactly the same, but this work[https://www.econ.cam.ac.uk/research-files/repec/cam/pdf/cwpe2171.pdf]is <https://www.econ.cam.ac.uk/research-files/repec/cam/pdf/cwpe2171.pdf%5Dis> highly related to what I intend to achieve. I would like to get if models with mediation paths added improved the model performance in terms of variance explained, and how share of variance explained of the outcome variable is changed by adding mediation paths.
> >
